page: Amazon Web Services r8idb.xlarge is an eighth-generation memory-optimized instance operating on the AWS Nitro hypervisor architecture. The instance is powered by a 3.9 GHz Intel x86_64 processor, providing 4 dedicated virtual CPUs across 2 physical cores with 2 threads per core. System memory capacity is 32.0 GB, establishing an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio with 8.0 GB of RAM allocated per physical core.

Local I/O is supported by 237 GB of integrated direct-attached NVMe SSD instance storage. Networking capabilities provide a baseline bandwidth of 4 Gbps, and zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses are assigned to the instance by default. The configuration does not include discrete GPU hardware.

From an architectural efficiency standpoint, the bundled local NVMe storage provides rapid temporary data access without relying entirely on remote network volumes. However, standard instance storage is ephemeral, requiring external data persistence strategies for stateful operations. The resource profile supports memory-intensive workloads, distributed caching tiers, in-memory databases, and intermediate analytical processing tasks requiring low-latency scratch disks.
description: Amazon Web Services r8idb.xlarge is an x86_64 memory-optimized virtual machine powered by an Intel processor running at 3.9 GHz. Hosted on the AWS Nitro hypervisor, the instance supplies 4 dedicated vCPUs spanning 2 physical cores, coupled with 32.0 GB of system memory at an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU allocation. The hardware profile includes 237 GB of high-speed local NVMe SSD storage and a baseline network bandwidth of 4 Gbps. The instance does not provide dedicated GPU hardware. With its tight combination of elevated memory density, fixed local NVMe instance store volumes, and dedicated high-frequency compute threads, the r8idb.xlarge delivers balanced resources for latency-sensitive applications. Tradeoffs center on the ephemeral nature of local instance disks and the absence of discrete acceleration. Typical deployment fits include in-memory key-value databases, memory-bound caching systems, relational database management engines, and real-time analytical data processing pipelines requiring swift local scratch capacity.
